phrases.say: Why does a chatbot forget what you told it an hour ago?
It's not memory loss. It's a window.
Every model can only read a fixed amount of text at once, counted in tokens. That's its context window.
Your whole chat, plus its own replies, has to fit inside.
When a conversation gets too long, the oldest parts fall out of the window, or get squeezed into a short summary.
And even inside the window, position matters.
In twenty twenty three, researchers found models use information best at the start and the end.

phrases.say: Details buried in the middle were used far worse.
They called it: lost in the middle.
So if something matters, put it at the start, or remind it near the end.

post.instagram_caption:
Why does a chatbot "forget" what you told it an hour ago?

It isn't memory loss. Every model can only read a fixed amount of text at once, measured in tokens: its context window. Your whole chat, plus its replies, has to fit. When a conversation runs long, the oldest parts fall out or get squeezed into a summary.

Even inside the window, position matters. A 2023 study, "Lost in the Middle", found models use information best at the start and the end of the input, and much worse in the middle.

The lesson: if something matters, put it at the start, or remind it near the end.

Source: Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle", arXiv, 2023.

post.youtube_description:
Chatbots don't forget like people do. Every model reads a fixed amount of text at once, its context window, and long chats push the oldest parts out or into a summary. A 2023 study also found models use information best at the start and end of their input, and much worse in the middle. Here's how it works and what to do about it.

Sources:
• Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts" (arXiv, 2023)
